articles.title: China’s extraordinary rise in science and how it will change the world
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03222-9The nation is on a trajectory to lead the world in science, a development that will reshape technological advancement, innovation and the balance of global power.
articles.content:
China’s President Xi Jinping is betting big on science. At a high-level meeting in Shanghai in April, he urged regional governments, universities and research institutes to strengthen the country’s fundamental research.

“We must seize opportunities, rise to challenges, put basic research high on the agenda,” he said.

Xi’s directive is part of a broad and long campaign by China to up its game in science and technology. Just a month earlier, the country’s leaders highlighted the importance of science in China’s latest five-year plan.

That policy blueprint calls for substantial investments in fundamental research and innovation, and pledges to accelerate the development of frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence, quantum applications and controlled nuclear fusion, by the end of this decade.

China’s AI research is booming. Where is it headed?

The fundamental-research push is China’s latest effort to grow its scientific and technological might — a campaign that started nearly 50 years ago and has accelerated drastically since 2000.

In 1978, when it opened itself to the world, China had almost no scientific presence on the global stage. Fewer than 120 scientific articles in international journals, or just 0.02% of the global total, were published by researchers in the country, according to Elsevier’s Scopus citation database.

But less than 50 years on, China has become a global scientific powerhouse and is on course to lead the world in research and development (R&D). Currently, it is one of the largest R&D spenders, leads in the number of patent applications and dominates research of dozens of crucial technologies, such as nuclear energy and synthetic biology. Its universities and institutes are rivalling conventional academic giants in the West and have topped the Nature Index chart for the first time.

Beyond numbers and rankings, China’s breakthroughs are commanding the world’s attention, from developing game-changing AI models to successfully retrieving rock samples from the far side of the Moon for the first time.

And its meteoric ascent in science could even accelerate in the coming years. The country’s current target is to raise its overall R&D expenditure, which includes the public and private sectors, by at least 7% per year between now and 2030, which is expected to translate into many billions of dollars of extra investments each year. This contrasts with forecasts for the United States, where President Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to cut funding for science and, critics say, has weakened research capabilities.

“China has the potential to fundamentally change the global landscape of science production, technology competition and the geopolitical centre of gravity,” says Yanbo Wang, a science-policy researcher at the University of Hong Kong. “For the West, if competing with Japan in the 1980s felt like weathering a storm, then China will bring a tsunami in the years to come.”

But before that happens, China will have to deal with some systemic concerns in its research ecosystem. Critics say that the go-fast approach has led to a widespread scientific-misconduct problem, which the government has been trying to tackle for more than a decade. And two deaths that occurred during clinical trials last year have led to questions about the regulations and ethics in cutting-edge biomedical research. Other issues — such as the threat of a slowing economy and geopolitical tensions — could also put the brakes on advances in science and technology.

Rising R&D

For the past three decades, China’s leaders have put science and education at the centre of the country’s effort to boost its prosperity. The country’s overall R&D spending increased by roughly 100 times during the period. Over the past ten years, its spending grew by more than 10% year-on-year on average, according to statistics published by the Chinese government.

China’s surge vastly outstrips spending increases in other nations, according to figures compiled by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In 2024, China overtook the United States — a country widely considered the world’s leader in scientific discovery and technology innovation since the end of the Second World War — to become the world’s largest spender in gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD). The measure includes all spending by public and private sectors.

The OECD adjusted the two countries’ GERD values using purchasing power parity (PPP), which takes into account the fact that goods and services in China are cheaper than they are in the United States. But China-based researchers warn against jumping straight to the conclusion that China is now the world’s largest R&D spender owing to the complexity of comparing the R&D spending of two nations. When adjusted by exchange rates, another way of doing the calculations, China’s R&D spending was about half of that of the United States in 2024, compared with 8% in 2004, according to the OECD (see ‘Money matters’).

One of China’s biggest advantages in scientific development is its ability to implement long-term plans and follow them through consistently, says Zhang Lin, a science-policy researcher at Wuhan University in China.

“China’s centralized system allows it to focus resources on long-term scientific goals more effectively,” Zhang says. China’s leadership can sustain investments over long periods of time in strategic scientific areas, such as quantum communications, she says. By contrast, political changes in the United States can cause the country to pivot from one priority to another.

For many researchers, what matters isn’t China’s exact ranking but its strong upward trajectory. China’s ballooning R&D investment shows that it is trying to move from being a producer of goods to a producer of knowledge and frontier technologies, says Hao Bin, an economist at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, China.

“Instead of competing mainly through its advantages in low labour costs, China is increasingly competing through its technological abilities, innovation ecosystems and the control of technologies,” Hao says.

A clear example is China’s long-term plan to develop its semiconductor industry, according to Hao. In 2014, China launched a state-backed investment fund to support the industry with an initial funding round of roughly 100 billion yuan (almost US$16.3 billion at the time). The fund, combined with coordinated industrial policies, has enabled China to build its capabilities throughout the semiconductor supply chain, from designing chips to manufacturing chip-making equipment, Hao says.

Since the United States imposed a sweeping ban on the sales of advanced semiconductor chips to China in 2022, the Chinese government has stepped up its support, Hao says. The third round of the fund, launched in 2024, is expected to hand out 344 billion yuan (roughly $50 billion) to companies in the semiconductor industry.

Other strategic areas that China has focused on are biotechnology and biomedicine. The government put a growing emphasis on the R&D of original drugs and translational medicine, which seeks to develop clinical treatments from fundamental research.

The AI race

In early 2025, a small AI company called DeepSeek sent shock waves through global markets when it released a large language model (LLM) that rivalled the performance of the dominant tools developed by US tech giants. DeepSeek, based in Hangzhou, China, achieved this breakthrough at a fraction of the cost spent by Western companies and using many fewer computing resources.

This type of innovation by a private company grew out of sustained support from the central government. Historically, state-run universities and research institutes led R&D efforts in China. But since 2010, when the government started a national campaign to nurture a group of ‘strategic emerging industries’ — which range from electric vehicles to pharmaceuticals — private firms have been playing an increasingly important part in driving the country’s innovation.

The US is the world’s science superpower — but for how long?

“Companies have become more and more active in R&D in China because they realize innovation is key to securing more market shares,” Hao says.

The Chinese government says it now hopes that private companies can play an even bigger part. Its latest five-year plan pledges to put more power and resources in the hands of such firms to improve the country’s innovation, education and research ecosystems. The move stems partly from the R&D success that some Chinese companies have demonstrated in key technologies in the past few years, from batteries to AI, according to researchers.

AI has served as a “confidence booster” for China in terms of where it stands in the global technological competition, says Meicen Sun, an information scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign.

Space exploration is another area in which China has been gaining confidence. In 2022, it finished building its own space station, Tiangong or Heavenly Palace, after three decades of planning and building.

That was a milestone for China’s space programme, says Xie Gengxin, who studies environmental application in space at Chongqing University in China. “It means that China is now capable of conducting mid-to-long-term research in space,” he says.

Another achievement for China was becoming the first nation to land a rover on the far side of the Moon. It intends to land astronauts on the lunar surface by 2030 and launch a mission to Mars in 2028 that aims to bring samples back to Earth three years later.

China now views building its progress in space research as a key national strategy, and Xie expects the government to channel plenty of resources into the sector, from finance to talent. Yuqi Qian, a planetary geologist at the University of Hong Kong, agrees that China considers its space exploration as a long-term effort to boost its technological sovereignty and national power, rather than a short-term geopolitical race to beat the United States.

“There is a narrative of an ongoing China–US space race in the US, but not in China,” says Qian, who is participating in China’s lunar and deep-space exploration programme.

Boosting basic research

China’s staunch scientific support is in part driven by its effort to reduce technological vulnerabilities and dependence, Hao says. Global events in the past decade, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the semiconductor restrictions imposed by the United States, exposed how relying on foreign technologies can become a strategic weakness for China, he says. During the pandemic, for example, many foreign experts left China and some scientific equipment could not be imported from abroad. This meant that the use of some technologies that relied on these specialists and equipment was affected, according to Hao. “So, R&D spending is increasingly serving as a national security goal.”

One step China has taken since 2018 — when Trump launched a trade war on China in his first term — is to boost its ability to make disruptive and original discoveries. This is widely considered a weak link in the country’s scientific system.

China pledges billion-dollar spending boost for science

China’s goal is to significantly increase its global impact in fundamental research — which is intended to develop knowledge rather than specific applications — by 2035, and make China a “major global scientific centre and innovation highland” by the middle of this century, said China’s State Council, the country’s highest administrative authority, in 2018.

But doing that won’t be easy. In 2024, funding for fundamental research accounted for just under 7% of China’s overall R&D budget, compared with 14.4% in the United States, according to calculations by Chris Martin, a science-data analyst and president of the Explorative Science Foundation, a non-profit organization in Christchurch, New Zealand, based on data from the OECD. China also lagged behind two of its neighbours, Japan (at 11.6%) and South Korea (at 14.7%). Even though the number rose to a record 7.08% in China last year, it failed to hit the 8% target laid out by China’s previous five-year plan that ended in 2025. The new five-year plan does not carry a funding target for it.

But, perhaps, a bigger obstacle is the country’s academic culture, which makes it hard for individual researchers to pursue long-term, curiosity-based projects, researchers warn.

Chinese researchers are constantly assessed on the basis of the number of papers they publish in a selection of influential journals and the amount of national grants they secure.

“So, the number of papers coming out of China has been growing quickly in recent years,” says Li Jizhen, a researcher of innovation policy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

Although the government launched a big reform in 2020, in the hope of improving its academic evaluation system, the number of published papers is still being used widely by Chinese universities to determine staff recruitment and promotion, several researchers have told Nature.

China is now the top-ranked country or territory for the number of papers its researchers publish in influential journals, having surpassed the United States in 2023, according to Nature Index, which tracks 178 journals in natural, applied, social and health sciences.

“But a large volume of papers won’t necessarily lead you to groundbreaking original discoveries that can win you a Nobel prize or a Turing Award, for example,” Li says. “The question is how to free researchers from hitting quantity-based targets and allow them to confidently conduct long-term research that may or may not succeed.”

The pressure to publish is also contributing to problems with research integrity in China, say some specialists who study this issue. A Nature investigation of article retractions found that between 2014 and 2024, nearly 60% of retracted papers included authors with affiliations to China.
articles.reasoning: The article reports China's significant and sustained investment in science and technology, leading to breakthroughs in AI, space exploration, and other frontier technologies. This development has broad global significance, reshaping technological advancement and innovation with measurable benefits for society. The article provides detailed context on China's rise, strategic plans, and challenges, focusing on a single main topic.
articles.personality_title: China’s growing leadership in science reshapes global technology
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Over the past 50 years, China has transformed from a minor player in global science to one of the world’s biggest investors and innovators in research and development (R&D). The country aims to become a global leader in science by 2035, focusing on technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, and space exploration.

**What happened** – China’s government, led by President Xi Jinping, has made science a top priority with strong support for universities, research institutes, and private companies. The country now spends more on R&D than any other nation when adjusted for purchasing power. Chinese researchers have produced more scientific papers than any other country and made advances such as landing a rover on the Moon’s far side and building its own space station. Private companies like DeepSeek have also developed AI tools that compete with those from the United States.

**Impact** – China’s rise in science changes how the world develops new technologies. Its steady investment allows long-term plans that other countries might struggle to maintain. This shift means China is moving from making products cheaply to leading in creating new knowledge and technologies. For example, China is building its own semiconductor industry to reduce dependence on foreign technology, which is crucial for national security.

**What’s next step** – China plans to keep increasing R&D spending by about 7% each year until 2030. It aims to improve basic research and innovation, though challenges remain, such as improving research ethics and encouraging scientists to pursue long-term projects without pressure to publish many papers. China also intends to expand its space missions, including plans to send astronauts to the Moon by 2030 and return samples from Mars.

articles.title: Atomic-scale spin sensing of a 2D d-wave altermagnet via helical tunneling
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11257-1Atomic-scale spin sensing of a 2D d-wave altermagnet via helical tunneling
articles.content: Altermagnets simultaneously possess momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting and zero net magnetization (1-6). Their defining crystalline symmetry connects opposite-spin sublattices in real space and imposes alternating spin polarization on the symmetry-related electronic states in momentum space (1-3). Identifying such an order and its associated spin response therefore calls for atomic-scale spin-sensitive measurements in both real and momentum space, an experimental milestone yet to be achieved. Here we show that the helical edge modes of the higher-order topological insulator α-Bi 4 Br 4 can serve as a spin-selective scanning tunnelling microscopy probe of the two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic order in the surface layer of KV 2 Se 2 O. Atomically registered mapping reveals the spatial relationship between the two V sublattices and a density-wave lattice modulation, as well as real-space patterns consistent with the checkerboard antiferromagnetic order. Field-dependent spectroscopy further finds opposite energy shifts of the unidirectional quasiparticle excitations extending along two orthogonal crystal axes and a predominantly out-of-plane magnetic response. In momentum space, spin-sensitive quasiparticle interference imaging reveals a bias-reversing d-wave anisotropy between the symmetry-paired X and Y valleys. These results provide converging evidence for two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetism on the surface of KV 2 Se 2 O and demonstrate helical-edge-mode tunnelling as a route for atomic-scale spin sensing in quantum materials.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in atomic-scale spin sensing of a novel 2D d-wave altermagnet using helical tunneling, demonstrating a new method for spin-sensitive measurements in quantum materials. This advancement has broad implications for quantum technology and materials science, offering a new tool for exploring and manipulating quantum states with potential large-scale technological impact.
articles.personality_title: Scientists achieve atomic-scale spin sensing of a new 2D magnetic material
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists study tiny magnetic effects in special materials called altermagnets. These materials have a unique type of magnetism that changes depending on the direction of electrons, but overall, they don’t act like regular magnets.

**What happened** – A team of researchers used a special technique involving helical tunneling, which uses tiny edge currents in a related material, to measure the spin (a magnetic property) of electrons in a two-dimensional (2D) d-wave altermagnet called KV2Se2O. This method allowed them to see details at the scale of individual atoms and map how spins are arranged across the material.

**Impact** – This is the first time scientists have been able to directly measure and map these complex magnetic patterns in both real space (where atoms are) and momentum space (how electrons move). It helps us understand how electrons behave in new quantum materials, which could be important for future technology like quantum computers or advanced electronics.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will likely use this new spin sensing method to explore other materials with unusual magnetic properties. This could lead to discovering new magnetic behaviors and help design devices that control electron spins more precisely.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new atomic-scale method reveals detailed magnetic patterns in a novel 2D material, opening doors to better understanding and using quantum magnetic effects.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques réalisent la détection du spin à l’échelle atomique d’un nouveau matériau magnétique 2D
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient de petits effets magnétiques dans des matériaux spéciaux appelés altermagnétiques. Ces matériaux ont un type unique de magnétisme qui change selon la direction des électrons, mais dans l’ensemble, ils ne se comportent pas comme des aimants classiques.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs a utilisé une technique spéciale appelée tunnelage hélicoïdal, qui utilise de minuscules courants de bord dans un matériau lié, pour mesurer le spin (une propriété magnétique) des électrons dans un altermagnétique 2D en forme d’onde d appelé KV2Se2O. Cette méthode leur a permis de voir des détails à l’échelle des atomes et de cartographier la disposition des spins dans le matériau.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que les scientifiques peuvent mesurer et cartographier directement ces motifs magnétiques complexes à la fois dans l’espace réel (où se trouvent les atomes) et dans l’espace des moments (comment bougent les électrons). Cela aide à comprendre le comportement des électrons dans de nouveaux matériaux quantiques, ce qui pourrait être important pour des technologies futures comme les ordinateurs quantiques ou l’électronique avancée.

**Étape suivante** – Les chercheurs vont probablement utiliser cette nouvelle méthode de détection du spin pour explorer d’autres matériaux avec des propriétés magnétiques inhabituelles. Cela pourrait conduire à la découverte de nouveaux comportements magnétiques et aider à concevoir des dispositifs qui contrôlent les spins des électrons avec plus de précision.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle méthode à l’échelle atomique révèle des motifs magnétiques détaillés dans un nouveau matériau 2D, ouvrant la voie à une meilleure compréhension et utilisation des effets magnétiques quantiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos logran detectar el giro a escala atómica de un nuevo material magnético 2D
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian pequeños efectos magnéticos en materiales especiales llamados altermagnetos. Estos materiales tienen un tipo único de magnetismo que cambia según la dirección de los electrones, pero en general, no actúan como imanes normales.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores usó una técnica especial llamada tunelado helicoidal, que utiliza pequeñas corrientes en los bordes de un material relacionado, para medir el giro (una propiedad magnética) de los electrones en un altermagneto bidimensional (2D) en forma de onda d llamado KV2Se2O. Este método les permitió ver detalles a escala atómica y mapear cómo se organizan los giros en el material.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que los científicos pueden medir y mapear directamente estos patrones magnéticos complejos tanto en el espacio real (dónde están los átomos) como en el espacio de momento (cómo se mueven los electrones). Esto ayuda a entender cómo se comportan los electrones en nuevos materiales cuánticos, lo que podría ser importante para tecnologías futuras como computadoras cuánticas o electrónica avanzada.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores probablemente usarán este nuevo método de detección de giro para explorar otros materiales con propiedades magnéticas inusuales. Esto podría llevar a descubrir nuevos comportamientos magnéticos y ayudar a diseñar dispositivos que controlen los giros de los electrones con mayor precisión.

**Frase clave** – Un nuevo método a escala atómica revela patrones magnéticos detallados en un nuevo material 2D, abriendo puertas para entender y usar mejor los efectos magnéticos cuánticos.

articles.title: Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11255-3Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
articles.content: Polyethylene (PE) accounts for more than a quarter of all plastic produced, owing to its exceptional material properties and scalable production.1 However, pristine PE lacks critical properties, such as adhesion, that are needed for many additional commercial applications.2 Selective post-polymerization functionalization of PE can impart properties that are absent in the pristine polymer, but global functionalization in a uniform medium perturbs bulk properties.3–5 Here, we demonstrate catalytic functionalization of solid PE at a solid–liquid interface. The resulting materials possess enhanced surface properties while maintaining bulk properties, such as melting temperature or tensile strength. The method selectively converts methylene units to ketones with just 0.001 mol% iron catalyst below 80 °C with inexpensive oxidants. PE functionalized at the solid–liquid interface adheres to polar surfaces up to 90-fold more strongly than does pristine PE and up to 4-fold more strongly than does PE functionalized in a uniform medium at a comparable level. We demonstrate that the surface ketones can be modified to enhance adhesive strength further and that the augmented surface properties persist for longer than they do after other unselective functionalizations. Thus, selective C–H bond functionalization at the solid–liquid interface produces materials inaccessible by bulk functionalization methods or by traditional surface oxidations.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in the selective catalytic oxidation of polyethylene surfaces, enhancing adhesion properties without compromising bulk material qualities. This innovation has broad implications for improving plastic materials used widely in industry, potentially enabling more sustainable and versatile applications.
articles.personality_title: New method improves plastic surface without weakening it
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Polyethylene is one of the most common plastics used worldwide because it is strong and easy to produce. However, it usually does not stick well to other materials, which limits how it can be used.

**What happened** – Scientists have developed a new way to change only the outside surface of polyethylene using a tiny amount of iron and a gentle chemical process. This method works at low temperatures and changes the surface to include special chemical groups called ketones without affecting the plastic inside.

**Impact** – The treated polyethylene sticks up to 90 times better to certain surfaces than untreated plastic, and better than other methods that try to change the whole material. This means products made with this plastic could be stronger and more reliable without losing their original qualities like strength and heat resistance.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely explore how this surface treatment can be used in real products, such as packaging, coatings, or medical devices, and may test other ways to improve the surface further.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new, gentle chemical method improves the surface of polyethylene to make it stick better without weakening the plastic itself.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle méthode améliore la surface du plastique sans l’affaiblir
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le polyéthylène est l’un des plastiques les plus utilisés dans le monde grâce à sa solidité et sa facilité de production. Cependant, il n’adhère généralement pas bien à d’autres matériaux, ce qui limite ses usages.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont développé une nouvelle façon de modifier seulement la surface extérieure du polyéthylène en utilisant une très petite quantité de fer et un procédé chimique doux. Cette méthode fonctionne à basse température et ajoute des groupes chimiques appelés cétone sans changer l’intérieur du plastique.

**Impact** – Le polyéthylène traité colle jusqu’à 90 fois mieux à certaines surfaces que le plastique non traité, et mieux que d’autres méthodes qui modifient tout le matériau. Cela signifie que les produits faits avec ce plastique pourraient être plus solides et fiables sans perdre leurs qualités originales comme la résistance et la température de fusion.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont probablement tester cette méthode sur des produits réels, comme des emballages, des revêtements ou des dispositifs médicaux, et chercher d’autres moyens d’améliorer encore la surface.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle méthode chimique douce améliore la surface du polyéthylène pour qu’il adhère mieux sans affaiblir le plastique lui-même.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.summary: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
articles.content:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."

This research has broad societal implications for how AI is understood and discussed, which can influence ethical AI development and public policy.
articles.personality_title: Study shows people see AI as aware but not conscious, even when it acts like humans
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more advanced, it often behaves in ways that seem human-like, such as responding to sounds or recognizing emotions. This has raised questions about whether people think AI can be conscious like humans.

**What happened** – Researchers at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich conducted a study with nearly 1,100 participants. They compared how people judged humans and AI acting the same way. Participants read descriptions of characters—either humans or AI—with different levels of responsiveness to their surroundings. They then rated how conscious or aware these characters seemed.

**Impact** – The study found that while people thought AI was aware of its environment almost as much as humans, they did not believe AI was conscious. Even the most responsive AI was seen as less conscious than the least responsive human. This shows that people clearly separate the idea of AI acting intelligently from having a conscious mind. It also reveals that words like “consciousness” and “awareness” carry different meanings for people.

**What’s next step** – Understanding how people view AI can help improve how we talk about these technologies. The researchers suggest using careful language to avoid confusion about what AI can actually do. This insight could influence how AI is developed, explained, and regulated in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – People recognize AI’s ability to notice and respond to things but still see a clear difference between AI and human consciousness, even when their actions are the same.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une étude montre que les gens voient l’IA comme consciente de son environnement, mais pas comme consciente elle-même
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’intelligence artificielle (IA) devient de plus en plus avancée et agit souvent comme un humain, par exemple en réagissant aux sons ou en reconnaissant les émotions. Cela soulève la question de savoir si les gens pensent que l’IA peut être consciente comme un humain.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université Ludwig Maximilian de Munich ont réalisé une étude avec près de 1 100 participants. Ils ont comparé la façon dont les gens jugeaient des humains et des IA qui agissaient de la même manière. Les participants ont lu des descriptions de personnages – humains ou IA – avec différents niveaux de réactivité à leur environnement. Ils ont ensuite évalué à quel point ces personnages semblaient conscients ou conscients de leur environnement.

**Impact** – L’étude a montré que, même si les gens pensent que l’IA est presque aussi consciente de son environnement que les humains, ils ne croient pas que l’IA soit consciente. Même l’IA la plus réactive était considérée comme moins consciente que l’humain le moins réactif. Cela montre que les gens distinguent clairement le fait qu’une IA agit de façon intelligente et le fait d’avoir un esprit conscient. Cela révèle aussi que les mots « conscience » et « conscience de » ont des sens différents pour les gens.

**Prochaine étape** – Comprendre comment les gens perçoivent l’IA peut aider à mieux parler de ces technologies. Les chercheurs suggèrent d’utiliser un langage précis pour éviter toute confusion sur ce que l’IA peut vraiment faire. Cette idée pourrait influencer la façon dont l’IA est développée, expliquée et réglementée à l’avenir.

**En une phrase** – Les gens reconnaissent que l’IA peut remarquer et réagir à son environnement, mais ils voient toujours une différence claire entre l’IA et la conscience humaine, même lorsque leurs actions sont identiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Estudio muestra que la gente ve a la IA como consciente de su entorno, pero no como consciente en sí misma
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La inteligencia artificial (IA) se está volviendo cada vez más avanzada y a menudo actúa como un humano, por ejemplo, respondiendo a sonidos o reconociendo emociones. Esto genera la pregunta de si las personas creen que la IA puede ser consciente como un humano.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad Ludwig Maximilian de Múnich realizaron un estudio con casi 1,100 participantes. Compararon cómo las personas juzgaban a humanos y a IA que actuaban de la misma manera. Los participantes leyeron descripciones de personajes—humanos o IA—con diferentes niveles de respuesta a su entorno. Luego evaluaron qué tan conscientes o atentos parecían estos personajes.

**Impacto** – El estudio encontró que, aunque las personas creen que la IA está casi tan consciente de su entorno como los humanos, no creen que la IA sea consciente. Incluso la IA más receptiva fue vista como menos consciente que el humano menos receptivo. Esto muestra que las personas separan claramente el comportamiento inteligente de una IA y la posesión de una mente consciente. También revela que las palabras “conciencia” y “atención” tienen significados diferentes para las personas.

**Próximo paso** – Entender cómo las personas ven la IA puede ayudar a mejorar cómo hablamos de estas tecnologías. Los investigadores sugieren usar un lenguaje cuidadoso para evitar confusiones sobre lo que la IA realmente puede hacer. Esta idea podría influir en cómo se desarrolla, explica y regula la IA en el futuro.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las personas reconocen la capacidad de la IA para notar y responder, pero aún ven una diferencia clara entre la IA y la conciencia humana, incluso cuando sus acciones son iguales.
